action.priority: Least warning time (2 of 3): nine in ten were outside the map and the Inde is a small, flashy river — fewer people than Liège, but the shortest lead time.
action.shelter: 91 % of the people the water reached are within 500 m of a public building on safe ground (median 416 m) — shelter is close here.
action.lever: The map misses this valley (the Inde, a small river), so a river dyke will not help: the levers are flash-flood warning, local protection, and managed retreat of the most exposed homes.
action.since: The Eifel-Rur water board applied in 2023 for two retention basins on the Vicht upstream of Stolberg (Roetgen-Rott and Mulartshütte); their approval status is not confirmed. German reconstruction aid is documented for North Rhine-Westphalia as a whole, not for the Aachen region.

action.priority: Evacuate first (1 of 3): the farthest from a shelter (855 of 1,356 have none within 500 m), and the Vesdre rises fast.
action.shelter: Only 37 % of the people the water reached are within 500 m of a public building on safe ground (median ~1.1 km) — shelter is far for many; and 45 schools and 2 hospitals or care homes sit inside the 1-in-100 zone themselves.
action.lever: On the Meuse the defences hold — warn and open shelters, not a bigger dyke. On the Vesdre the water is outside the map (a small river): flash warning, local protection, managed retreat.
action.since: Vesdre strategic scheme (2023), resilient bank works, Eupen dam flood reserve raised 2.8→7 M m³ — but only one Walloon reservoir dam has an emergency plan (2025).

action.priority: Lower (3 of 3): most people are inside the map, the defences hold, and the Maas gives more warning time.
action.shelter: 60 % of the people the water reached are within 500 m of a public building on safe ground (median 722 m).
action.lever: Mostly inside the map and the defences largely hold — the levers are warning, shelter, and the cross-border Meuse signal.
action.since: Dutch Limburg programme (Waterveiligheid en Ruimte Limburg) and the Beleidstafel actions — 50 of 80 done by 2026.

how_we_counted: The water is what Copernicus EMS outlined as flooded area or flood trace on its first map of each area (EMSR517/518/520). Later monitoring maps add water seen days afterwards; they are shown as small print, never mixed into a headline.
Residents are GHS-POP 2020 (E2020) counts, each ~1 km cell weighted by the share of it under the observed water, on a 20 m equal-area grid (EPSG:3035).
Outside the 1-in-100-year zone means the 20 m cell is dry in the JRC river flood hazard map for that return period (depth 0 or no data).
Buildings are GHS-OBAT points inside the observed water; "destroyed" is the Copernicus analysts' damage grade, available only for German grading maps.
Country totals are counted on the union of the areas, cell by cell and building by building, so two maps over the same valley are not counted twice.
Reproduced independently in the case notebook, computed from the data bucket, not copied from this page.
warnings: Do not triage on the 1-in-100-year map alone. It models only large rivers without dikes; much of the 2021 water came from small rivers and runoff, and whole valleys flooded outside it.
Outside a mapped area means not mapped, not dry. Absence of colour on a map is missing data, not safety.
Works funded are not works finished. "About 880 km" of resilient Vesdre banks is a 2022 plan; no official source confirms how many kilometres are built.
A 1-in-100-year design is not a guarantee. The Ahrweiler district counts as protected to the 1-in-100-year flood, and the Ahr flooded in 2021.
Shelter distances here are straight-line floors. Real walking is longer and bridges may be cut, so treat the reach figures as optimistic.
In 2021 the forecast existed days ahead; the last mile failed. Warn people with an action, not just a signal.

rows.what: Alert at the first EFAS notice, with the worst case and one action. Say how bad it could get and what to do; the 10 July 2021 notice never said it would be far worse by the 14th. Warn first where warning time is shortest (the Vesdre valley, Eschweiler), then the zones de secours, the Eupen and Gileppe dam operators and the Meuse authorities across the border.
rows.who: Anna, before the forecast rain arrives.
rows.how: Cell Broadcast (BE-Alert, NL-Alert, DE-Alert); staff time.

rows.what: Give every street a meeting point. In Liège 855 of the 1,356 people the 2021 water reached had no dry public building within 500 m: ask the mayors to name, street by street, the nearest dry building as the meeting point and put it in the alert ("leave the valley floor, go to ..."); help first those who cannot act alone (the elderly were overrepresented among the dead, Thieken et al., 2026); where none is within walking reach, plan transport.
rows.who: Anna, with the mayors, this week.
rows.how: The alert message and this tool's map of dry buildings; staff time.

rows.what: One border, one picture, before 2027. The decision-makers differ in each country (the provincial governor in Liège, the safety regions in Dutch Limburg, the Städteregion Aachen), and their reports cannot be compared: Belgium has no damage grading, Belgian Limburg no 2021 satellite map. Agree one shared picture (rain, river flow, dam releases), one alert trigger, common data standards so reports compare, and map the small rivers the European map leaves out (below about 150 km²). Then the right lever: warning and meeting points, not a bigger dyke, on big rivers; flash warning, local protection and managed retreat on small ones. Of the €46 bn of 2021 flood losses in Europe only €11 bn were insured (Munich Re, 2022).
rows.who: Anna, with her counterparts in Dutch Limburg and the Aachen region, through EMRIC (the Euregio Meuse-Rhine crisis cooperation) and the International Meuse Commission, for the 2027 plan review.
rows.how: Floods Directive Article 8(2), one coordinated plan for the Meuse district, and the Article 14 review (Article 8(5) if a State cannot resolve an issue): no new body.

next_steps.what: Close the last mile of the warning chain: push a public cell-broadcast alert carrying a magnitude and an action ("leave the valley floor"), wired to the European flood forecast, not just a generic warning.
next_steps.who: Anna triggers it; national and regional civil-protection authorities send it, before the forecast rain arrives.
next_steps.basis: The European flood forecast warned national authorities from 10 July 2021, yet 29–35 % of residents got no warning and up to half of those warned did not know what to do (peer-reviewed survey of the July 2021 flood, 2023); the cell-broadcast basis exists since February 2022.

next_steps.what: Do not triage on the 1-in-100-year map alone: trigger on the observed 2021 footprint joined with that map, and treat small rivers and runoff as unmapped risk.
next_steps.who: The crisis coordinator, for this event.
next_steps.basis: The hazard map models only large rivers; in the Aachen region about nine in ten of the people the water reached were outside it (this tool's own result).

next_steps.what: Pre-activate the nearest safe public buildings as shelters for the places where residents are far from one.
next_steps.basis: The shelter reach per place shown in this tool.

next_steps.what: Finish an emergency plan for every reservoir dam, not only the one that has it, and publish the forecast-driven operating rule for the Vesdre dams.
next_steps.who: Provincial governors and the Walloon waterways administration.
next_steps.basis: The inquiry asked for a plan for every reservoir dam; only one exists; the independent review (6 December 2021) asked for a legal dam-safety framework and forecast-driven operation.

next_steps.what: Publish the updated Vesdre strategic scheme, give the hazard map real weight in building permits, and report the kilometres of resilient bank actually rebuilt, not only the plan.
next_steps.who: The Walloon territory and environment administration.
next_steps.basis: The scheme (2023) binds no commune and its promised update is still unpublished; "about 880 km" is a 2022 plan.

next_steps.what: Harmonise the regional flood-map viewers, put water depths on every hazard map, state climate change, and set quantified, time-bound objectives before the next plan.
next_steps.who: The three Belgian regions, before the 22 December 2027 plan review.
next_steps.basis: The Commission's assessment of Belgium under the Floods Directive (COM(2025) 2).

next_steps.what: Make cross-border coordination operational on the Meuse and the Vesdre–Rur, not only planned: shared data, joint forecasting, a common area vision.
next_steps.who: The Belgian, German and Dutch basin authorities.
next_steps.basis: The Dutch policy table asked for cooperation on all cross-border waters (2022); the Commission asks all three states for clearer international coordination (COM(2025) 2).

points: Parliamentary inquiry: 161 recommendations (187 with sub-recommendations), adopted March 2022; the three-year follow-up splits them 126 for the Region, 20 partly, 37 federal, with 19 more completed since October 2024 and 58 of 88 still in progress (Walloon Parliament, 2022; Walloon Government, 17 April 2025).

Reconstruction: repair cost about EUR 5.2 billion; emergency river-safety works on more than 1,000 bank sites, about 46 % done by mid-2022; resilient bank reconstruction funded (EUR 430 million recovery-plan axis 6, plus EUR 300 million of a EUR 1.1 billion EIB loan), with about 880 km along the Vesdre planned — a plan, not yet built (Commissariat à la Reconstruction, 1 July 2022; Walloon Government, 4 July 2022).

Prevention and planning: a circular on building in flood zones in force since 1 April 2022; the 2022–2027 flood-risk management plan (PGRI) approved 19 January 2023 with 671 local projects; EUR 71.2 million in resilience subsidies to communes (SPW, 2021–2023).

Dams and modelling: an independent review found the Vesdre valley floods from a 1-in-25-year event even with the Eupen dam, and asked for a legal dam-safety framework and forecast-driven operation (Stucky review, 6 December 2021); a whole-basin Vesdre model was delivered 19 March 2024 (ULiège ModRec).

Compensation and clean-up: the Region put in about EUR 1 billion so insurers cover 41 % and the Region 59 % of insured damage, and about 152,000 tonnes of flood waste were treated (Walloon Government, 4 July 2022).

Reconstruction fund of up to EUR 30 billion; about EUR 5.84 billion paid out by 31 December 2025. The federal government will not fund new flood-protection works from it (a task of the Länder) and points to EUR 127 million a year in the federal-Länder joint fund (German Bundestag, 27 February 2026).
Public warning: technical rules for Cell Broadcast / DE-Alert over mobile networks were published 23 February 2022, the legal basis in force since December 2021 (Bundesnetzagentur, 23 February 2022).

Prevention: the national flood-protection programme (NHWSP) for 2026–2035 is costed at about EUR 4 billion for the Länder, and the federal government is pursuing expanded mandatory natural-hazard insurance (German Bundestag, 27 February 2026).
Policy table on flooding: 21 recommendations, all accepted (19 December 2022); the safety model was widened from three to five layers, adding water-awareness and recovery.

Progress (final report, April 2026): of 80 actions, 50 done, 19 embedded in other programmes and 11 moved to a future national programme; the Limburg programme has a governing committee since November 2025 and plans built on 2100 climate projections (Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, 2022 and 2026).

Limburg is developing risk-based protection standards on one coherent methodology, and a public web tool lets residents look up flood risk by address (Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, 2026).
EU Solidarity Fund (December 2022): EUR 612.6 million to Germany, EUR 87.7 million to Belgium and EUR 4.7 million to the Netherlands (Decision (EU) 2023/68).

Implementation review (February 2025): only 8 of 21 assessed Member States link spatial planning and flood-risk management in law or policy, and nature-based solutions are in every plan but not yet taken up at scale; Belgium is asked for harmonised flood maps, water depths on every map and explicit climate change (European Commission, COM(2025) 2).

Reporting gaps: about 14,000 areas of potential significant flood risk are declared EU-wide, but five Member States had not submitted their plans by the September 2023 cut-off, and the Commission opened proceedings over late adoption (European Commission, COM(2025) 2).

conclusion: July 2021 showed that the flood map can miss many of the people a flood reaches, and that a forecast which reaches the authorities days ahead can still fail the people who must act. The border area is better prepared on paper than it is on the ground. Recommendation 1 is the action for this week's bulletin. Recommendations 2 and 3 close the shelter gaps and put each place's money on the lever its risk needs. The next window to act is the plan review of 22 December 2027.
limits: Built with AI, checked by people. AI wrote most of the code and drafted text. The team set every definition and weight, recomputed every figure from the organisers' data and checked it against the sources. No AI runs in this page. How AI was used, and where it was wrong, is in the team's AI sheet.

Scenarios, not a forecast. The maps are fixed flood scenarios (1-in-10, 1-in-100 and 1-in-500 years). They cannot say what happens in the next 5 to 10 hours if the rain keeps falling: that comes from the European flood forecast (EFAS) and the national flash-flood services, and linking their bulletins to this screening is the next step.
Satellite snapshots, not the peak. Copernicus maps show the water visible on one image, often a day or more after the crest. The true extent was larger.

Outside a mapped area means not mapped, not dry. Only the outlined areas were mapped; whole flooded valleys lie outside them. Liège's figures are a floor: neither satellite map shows water in Verviers or Pepinster, on the Vesdre.

Two readings, both stated. Liège is 13 % outside the map on the first satellite map and 34 % on the later, wider one. Shelter reach counts the buildings of all three countries (37 % within 500 m); the Belgian file alone gives 23 %. The case notebook recomputes the figures independently on the organisers' data, and an automatic test checks that they match.

Two kinds of maps. Delineation maps, drawn semi-automatically from radar, stop at building walls and miss water between houses; grading maps, drawn by analysts, carry the water through the towns. Belgium has only delineation maps, which is why its building count is low.

Population is a model, on two grids. The July 2021 figures use GHS-POP 2020 (E2020), as the organisers ask for a 2021 event; the European figures use GHS-POP 2025 (E2025, 1 km), the grid the EU-wide layer is built on. Both spread residents evenly within each ~1 km cell and do not know who was home in July 2021.

Design standards are not guarantees. The European figures assume no dikes. The JRC protection layer counts every exposed resident of the Ahrweiler district as protected against the 1-in-100-year flood, and the Ahr flooded in 2021.

The hazard map covers large rivers only. The JRC map models rivers with catchments of 150 km² and more, without dikes, and no surface runoff or small streams: much of the 2021 damage came from exactly those.
Permanent water is excluded from the map scores (it is wet in every map and would count as a free hit); residents beside it are still counted.

Plan review date: Directive 2007/60/EC (Floods Directive), Article 14(3): flood risk management plans "shall be reviewed, and if necessary updated ... by 22 December 2021 and every six years thereafter"; the next review falls on 22 December 2027.

decision.actor: Anna — crisis coordinator of the Liège–Limburg–Aachen border area
decision.lead: Warn before the water, tell every street where to go, one picture across the border.
points: Alert at the first EFAS notice, with the worst case and one action.
Give every street a meeting point.

before.when: When EFAS notifies (about four days ahead, as on 10 July 2021)
before.what: Put the dam operators, the river-flow services and the mayors on one shared picture. Name each street's meeting point: the nearest dry building.

before.who: Anna, with the province and the mayors
before.what: Send an alert that carries the worst case and how it could escalate, not a single level. Put the meeting point in the alert, Liège first, where residents have no dry building close by.

before.who: Anna triggers; civil protection sends (BE-Alert, NL-Alert, DE-Alert)
before.what: A Cell Broadcast that says what to do: "leave the valley floor". On the small rivers the map does not model, do not wait for the map.
They know what to do. This plan ends where theirs begins.
